newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM tries to stifle early election rumours.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM tries to stifle early election rumours.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto struggled on Friday to quell growing media speculation that he plans to dissolve parliament and call a snap general election in October or early November.
Hashimoto denied front-page headlines in Japan's major dailies on Friday that he had acceded to calls from his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) for early elections for the Lower House of parliament.
"I have no plans to dissolve the Lower House for the time being because I must deal with such pending issues as Okinawa and economic recovery," Hashimoto told reporters at his official residence.

Hashimoto later said the same thing in a meeting with heads of coalition partners the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake in an effort to reassure those groups, widely thought to be less prepared for polls than the LDP.
"The prime minister told us he was annoyed by today's media reports," said Sakigake chief Shoichi Ide after the meeting.
Three major dailies, the liberal Asahi Shimbun, the conservative Yomiuri Shimbun and the business newspaper Nihon Keizai Shimbun said Hashimoto would call polls between October 20 and November 10.
Hashimoto does not have to call elections until mid-1997, when the four-year term of the current Lower House expires.

The newspapers cited unnamed senior officials in the ruling coalition as saying Hashimoto, believed to have been planning to wait until after January to dissolve parliament, had changed his mind under growing pressure from within the LDP, which has set its candidate lists and is spoiling for early polls.

The coalition leaders cited concern about a campaign by the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) against an unpopular plan to raise the consumption tax to five percent from the current three percent next April, the papers said.
Hashimoto took office in January at the head of a three-party coalition of the LDP, the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake.

Sakigake and the Socialist Democrats have in recent weeks been troubled by disputes and defections over the question of the two moderate parties merging to form a larger bloc to better contest elections.

On Sunday, inhabitants of Okinawa, Japan's southernmost island group, vote in a referendum on U.S. military bases -- a nonbinding poll predicted to give overwhelming support for Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota's campaign to trim bases in the prefecture.
Okinawa exploded in protest last year after the rape of a local schoolgirl by U.S. servicemen.
